title: Job 36:1–16
context: Elihu, the young speaker who entered in chapter 32 angry with both Job and the three friends (32:2–3), begins his last speech. He says he still has something to say on God's behalf. He describes God as mighty yet not despising anyone, and argues that God uses affliction to show people their pride, open their ears to instruction, and call them back from iniquity. This is Elihu's view of suffering as discipline. Interpreters evaluate Elihu differently: some see him as preparing the way for the LORD's speeches, noting that he is not named among those rebuked in 42:7; others see him as one more human counselor whose confidence outruns his knowledge. The book does not give a direct verdict on him, and one is not supplied here.

verses.arminianNotes: "Elihu also continued, and said," Arminian readers note that Elihu is the speaker here, in his fourth and final speech. His words are his own contribution to the debate, not the LORD's answer, which comes only in chapter 38.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the speaker is Elihu, not God or the narrator. Whatever value his words have, they must be weighed as one voice in the book, with the LORD's speeches still to come.

verses.text: “Bear with me a little, and I will show you; for I still have something to say on God’s behalf.
verses.arminianNotes: "Bear with me a little, and I will show you." Arminian readers see Elihu asking for patience because he believes he still has "something to say on God’s behalf." He presents himself as God's defender.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job had warned the friends against speaking deceitfully for God (13:7). Elihu claims to speak for God, and readers must test that claim rather than simply assume it.

verses.text: I will get my knowledge from afar, and will ascribe righteousness to my Maker.
verses.arminianNotes: "I will get my knowledge from afar." Arminian readers see Elihu claiming broad insight and promising to "ascribe righteousness to my Maker." His stated aim is to defend God's justice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that ascribing righteousness to God is a right goal, and both traditions affirm it. The open question is whether Elihu's explanation of Job's suffering is accurate, which the book does not directly settle.

verses.text: For truly my words are not false. One who is perfect in knowledge is with you.
verses.arminianNotes: "For truly my words are not false." Arminian readers note that Elihu claims that "One who is perfect in knowledge is with you," which many read as a bold claim about himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the same phrase is used of God in 37:16, "him who is perfect in knowledge." Readers differ on whether Elihu's self-description here is confident sincerity or overreach.

verses.text: “Behold, God is mighty, and doesn’t despise anyone. He is mighty in strength of understanding.
verses.arminianNotes: "Behold, God is mighty, and doesn’t despise anyone." Arminian readers welcome Elihu's insistence that God's power is joined with care. The mighty God does not look down on the weak.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God is "mighty in strength of understanding." His power is never blind force but wise. Both traditions treat this statement about God as shared ground, whatever one makes of Elihu's application.

verses.text: He doesn’t preserve the life of the wicked, but gives justice to the afflicted.
verses.arminianNotes: "He doesn’t preserve the life of the wicked, but gives justice to the afflicted." Arminian readers see Elihu stating God's justice in general terms, a truth the book affirms even when it is not visible right away.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this general principle is similar to what the three friends said, and that Job has questioned how it fits his experience (21:7 and 12:6). Elihu states it again without fully addressing Job's objection.

verses.text: He doesn’t withdraw his eyes from the righteous, but with kings on the throne, he sets them forever, and they are exalted.
verses.arminianNotes: "He doesn’t withdraw his eyes from the righteous." Arminian readers see God's watchful care over the righteous, whom he may raise up and set "with kings on the throne."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the comfort that God's eyes remain on the righteous. Job had felt God hiding his face (13:24); Elihu insists God has not looked away.

verses.text: If they are bound in fetters, and are taken in the cords of afflictions,
verses.arminianNotes: "If they are bound in fetters, and are taken in the cords of afflictions." Arminian readers see Elihu's view that even the righteous may fall into affliction, and that suffering can have a purpose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu begins his account of affliction as discipline here. This is his explanation, which differs from the friends' claim that suffering simply proves great guilt.

verses.text: then he shows them their work, and their transgressions, that they have behaved themselves proudly.
verses.arminianNotes: Elihu says, "then he shows them their work, and their transgressions." Arminian readers see Elihu claiming that God uses affliction to reveal hidden pride, giving people a chance to see themselves truly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note Elihu's emphasis on pride: "that they have behaved themselves proudly." He suggests that suffering exposes sins people would not otherwise recognize.

verses.text: He also opens their ears to instruction, and commands that they return from iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes: "He also opens their ears to instruction." Arminian readers see God calling people to respond: he "commands that they return from iniquity." Affliction is an invitation to repentance that people can heed or refuse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God's opening of the ear as his own gracious work that brings people to hear. Both traditions find shared ground in Hebrews 12:5–11, where the Lord's discipline is for his children's good.

verses.text: If they listen and serve him, they will spend their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasures.
verses.arminianNotes: "If they listen and serve him, they will spend their days in prosperity." Arminian readers see a real choice set before the afflicted, with blessing promised to those who listen and serve.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu presents listening and serving as the response to God's discipline. They also note that the book as a whole resists any simple rule that faithfulness always brings prosperity in this life.

verses.text: But if they don’t listen, they will perish by the sword; they will die without knowledge.
verses.arminianNotes: "But if they don’t listen, they will perish by the sword." Arminian readers see the other side of the choice: refusing God's instruction leads to death "without knowledge."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu sets out two paths, much as Proverbs does. They weigh it as Elihu's warning to Job, not as a description the narrator applies to Job's case.

verses.text: “But those who are godless in heart lay up anger. They don’t cry for help when he binds them.
verses.arminianNotes: "But those who are godless in heart lay up anger." Arminian readers see the godless refusing to cry for help even when God binds them. Their own resentment keeps them from turning back.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the godless respond to discipline with stored-up anger rather than prayer. The contrast is between affliction that humbles and affliction that hardens.

verses.text: They die in youth. Their life perishes among the unclean.
verses.arminianNotes: "They die in youth." Arminian readers see Elihu describing the tragic end of those who refuse to listen, whose lives perish "among the unclean."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu describes an outcome, not every case. The book itself has shown that early death or long life does not neatly match moral worth. Elihu's statement remains his own.

verses.text: He delivers the afflicted by their affliction, and opens their ear in oppression.
verses.arminianNotes: "He delivers the afflicted by their affliction." Arminian readers see Elihu's central claim: God can use suffering itself as the means of rescue, opening the ear "in oppression."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note this as the heart of Elihu's view: affliction can be a tool of grace. Both traditions affirm, with Hebrews 12:5–11, that God disciplines his children for their good, while reading this as Elihu's application to Job.

verses.text: Yes, he would have allured you out of distress, into a wide place, where there is no restriction. That which is set on your table would be full of fatness.
verses.arminianNotes: "Yes, he would have allured you out of distress, into a wide place." Arminian readers see Elihu telling Job that God wanted to lead him into freedom and abundance if he had responded rightly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Elihu now applies his view directly to Job. Whether his reading of Job's situation is right is part of the debate, since the reader knows from 1:1 that Job was blameless.
